title: If a Man Dies, Will He Live Again?
summary: Job reflects on the brevity and frailty of human life and asks God to look away and let him rest. A cut-down tree can sprout again, but a man lies down and does not rise. For a moment Job imagines God hiding him in Sheol until his anger passes and then calling him back, but the hope fades, and he ends with a picture of God wearing away human hope as water wears away stone.
story: Chapter 14 ends Job's long reply to his three friends (chapters 12 to 14) and closes the first round of the debate. In chapter 13 Job resolved to take his case to God and turned to address God directly. That direct address continues here, but the tone shifts from legal argument to meditation. Job steps back from his own case to look at the human condition itself, and in doing so he reaches toward a question the Old Testament rarely asks so openly: is death the end? The flicker of hope in verses 13-17 is the first of several moments in the book where Job reaches beyond the grave, a line of thought that returns more strongly in chapters 16 and 19.
historical:
Job's question in verse 14 must be read against the beliefs of his world. In most of the Old Testament, the dead go down to Sheol, a shadowy realm where there is no work, no praise of God, and no return (Psalm 6:5; Ecclesiastes 9:10). Hope for resurrection appears clearly only in a few later texts, above all Daniel 12:2, and more faintly in passages such as Isaiah 26:19. Israel's neighbors held various views. Egypt had an elaborate belief in a life beyond death for those judged worthy, with tombs, mummification, and funerary texts. Mesopotamian literature, in contrast, pictured the underworld as a dark land of no return, where the dead ate dust. Job's picture of Sheol is closer to that Mesopotamian gloom than to Egyptian confidence.

That is what makes verses 13-17 so remarkable. Job does not assume resurrection. He imagines it as a wish, a thing God could do if he chose, and then lets the thought go.
cultural:
The tree in verses 7-9 would be familiar to anyone who farmed in the eastern Mediterranean. Olive trees, sycamores, and others can be cut down to the stump and still send up new shoots from the root, sometimes after years, once rain comes. Isaiah uses the same picture of a stump sprouting to describe the hope of a new king from the line of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1). Job's point is the reverse: a tree has that hope, but a man does not.

The hired hand in verse 6 returns from chapter 7: a laborer who at least has a day's end and wages to look forward to. The sealed bag in verse 17 draws on the ancient practice of tying up and sealing items for safekeeping, such as valuables or records, so that no one could open them. Job pictures God sealing up his sins in a bag and putting them away, not to preserve them as evidence but to be done with them.
literary: The chapter is a carefully built meditation in four parts. Verses 1-6 describe human life as short, troubled, and fragile, like a flower or a shadow, and ask God to look away. Verses 7-12 contrast the tree that sprouts again with the man who does not rise. Verses 13-17 are a daring wish that God would hide Job in Sheol and later remember him, call him, and cover his sin. Verses 18-22 collapse that hope with images of erosion: mountains crumbling, stones worn away by water. The word hope frames the whole: there is hope for a tree (verse 7), but God destroys the hope of man (verse 19). The famous opening line, “Man, who is born of woman, is short of days and full of trouble,” has been read at funerals for centuries.

outline.t: Human life is brief: look away and let him rest
A tree can sprout again, but man lies down
A wish: hide me in Sheol and remember me
As water wears stone, you destroy man's hope

doctrines.note: Human beings are frail, mortal, and born into trouble. Job's meditation takes that mortality with full seriousness, and Scripture includes it as part of the truth about us.

Job asks the question to which the rest of the Bible gives its answer: if a man dies, will he live again? Job himself only glimpses the possibility, but his wish that God would call him back and long for the work of his hands becomes, in later revelation, the hope of resurrection.
Verse 4 asks who can bring clean from unclean. Job sees that human frailty includes moral impurity, and in verses 16-17 he longs for a God who would not keep track of sin but cover it.

words.note: Tiqvah, hope. It frames the chapter: there is hope for a tree (verse 7), but God destroys a man's hope (verse 19). The contrast between these two uses carries the chapter's emotional movement.

Chaliphah, a change or relief, used of a change of clothes or the relief of a soldier on duty. In verse 14 Job says he will wait all the days of his hard service until his renewal comes, picturing a soldier waiting for the one who will take over his watch.

Tseror, a bag or bundle tied shut. In verse 17 Job pictures his transgression sealed in a bag. The same word appears in Abigail's blessing that David's life would be bound in the bundle of the living (1 Samuel 25:29).

Tame, unclean, a word from Israel's purity laws describing what cannot enter God's presence. Job's question in verse 4 about bringing clean from unclean asks whether anything born of human beings can be pure before God.

christ: Job's question, “When a man dies, will he live again?”, is one the New Testament answers directly, and it answers in the person of Jesus. Jesus told Martha that he is the resurrection and the life, and that whoever believes in him will live even though he dies (John 11:25). Paul describes Christ's resurrection as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first of a harvest still to come, and says that the perishable will put on the imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:53-54). Job's image of a tree cut down that sprouts again echoes Isaiah's promise of a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1), which the New Testament reads as fulfilled in Jesus. Job's wish that God would cover his sin and not keep track of it also looks ahead to the gospel of forgiveness. Job does not know these answers; he only asks the question well enough for them to be heard.

hard.q: Did Job believe in life after death?
hard.a: Interpreters answer differently, and the chapter itself holds both sides. On one hand, verses 10-12 and 18-22 speak of death as final: a man lies down and does not rise, until the heavens are no more. On the other, verses 13-17 express a longing that God would hide him in Sheol and then call him back, and verse 14 says he would wait until his renewal comes. Some read this as a real glimmer of faith in life beyond death, which grows into the confident statement of 19:25-27. Others read it as a wish Job himself considers impossible, since the next verses cancel it. A middle view sees Job as reaching for a hope that the Old Testament has not yet made clear, able to imagine it but not yet able to hold it. What all agree on is that the question is asked honestly, and that the rest of Scripture takes it up.

questions: Job contrasts the hope of a tree with the hopelessness of human death. How does the Christian hope of resurrection change the way you face your own mortality?
Job imagines God covering his sin and longing for the work of his hands. What does it mean to you that God might long for you in that way?
The chapter ends with erosion, hope worn away slowly. What small, steady pressures wear away your hope, and what renews it?
